headline: Jama was originally a Buddhist term, from Middle Chinese 邪魔, literally “wrong, evil, perverse” plus “devil, demon”.
Yurui appears to be derived from the archaic verb 揺る (yuru, “to shake, sway”).
Shodō is 書 (sho, “writing”) plus 道 (-dō, “-manship”).
Sofu is from Middle Chinese 祖父, the kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.
Chiji shortens 知某州事, “one who knows matters concerning the county/province”.
Nanboku is Middle Chinese 南北, literally “south and north”.
Kokyō is from Middle Chinese 故鄉 (MC kuH xjang), and its vowels shifted twice on the way.
Issō is 一 (ichi, “one”) plus 層 (sō, “layer”), shifted in pronunciation.
Kashi is the continuative stem of 貸す (kasu, “to lend, loan”).
Nerai is a nominalization of the stem of 狙う (nerau, “to aim”).
Katamaru is 固 (kata, “hard; solid”) plus -maru, “to become”.
Hageshii is cognate with the verb 励む (hagemu).
Yahari may be a hypercorrect back-formation from やっぱり (yappari).
Ishokujū is 衣 (i, “clothing”), 食 (shoku, “food”) and 住 (jū, “shelter”).
Taki, “waterfall”, is simply listed as from Old Japanese.
Kanarazushimo is 必ず (kanarazu, “certainly”) plus the emphatic しも (shimo), the same one seen in 誰しも (dareshimo).
Atsumari is the continuative stem of 集まる (atsumaru).
Tadashii is 直 (tada, “straight; direct; straightforward”) plus the adjective suffix し, first appearing in 858 CE.
Waribiki is the continuative stem of 割り引く (waribiku).
Kūchū, “sky”, was borrowed from Middle Chinese 空中, glossed “sky; air + middle”.
Asatte shifted from asate, and the kanji spelling comes from myōgonichi.
Negai is the continuative stem of 願う (negau).
Akuma is Middle Chinese 惡魔, literally “bad, evil + demon”.
Yome has several theories, all reading it as よ (yo) plus 女 (me, “woman, female”); the yo may be 呼 (“to call out, invite”) or 弱 (“weak”).
Kotchi is a shift from the archaic pronoun こち (kochi).
Puro is an abbreviation for some borrowed words from English.
Yaya is a clipping of 稚児 (yayako).
Furaipan is borrowed from American English frypan.
Obasan is 小 (o, “small” or “little”) plus 母 (ba, “mother”) plus さん (san, honorific suffix).
Utsuru, “to be reflected”, is cognate with 移る.
